What goes here: A short stable reference (R-01, R-02...). Never reuse an ID after a risk is closed.
Why it earns its place: Lets people refer to a risk in a meeting or email without retyping the whole statement.

What goes here: One sentence in three parts: cause, event, consequence. "Reliance on a single supplier (cause) could lead to a production stoppage (event), delaying orders and triggering penalties (consequence)."
Why it earns its place: A topic like "supply chain" cannot be rated, owned or acted on. A statement can. This is the single highest-value discipline in the register.

What goes here: A short grouping: Operational, Compliance, Financial, Strategic, Continuity, People, Technology. Keep the list short.
Why it earns its place: Groups risks for reporting. Nothing more — resist the urge to build a taxonomy.

What goes here: A named individual. Never a department, never "TBC".
Why it earns its place: A risk owned by a function is owned by nobody. When something falls between two teams, a departmental owner gives everyone a reason to assume it sits elsewhere.

What goes here: What already reduces this risk today — not what you plan to do.
Why it earns its place: Stops effort being duplicated, and makes the rating honest. A risk with strong controls should rate lower than the same risk with none.

What goes here: 1-4 against the scale on the Scales sheet.
Why it earns its place: Half of the prioritisation. Keep the scale small so people cannot cluster everything in the middle.

What goes here: 1-4 against the scale on the Scales sheet. Define impact in your own terms before you start rating.
Why it earns its place: The other half. Generic words like "moderate" mean different things to different people in the same room.

What goes here: Calculated automatically (Likelihood x Impact). Do not overwrite the formula.
Why it earns its place: Drives ordering. Treat it as a sorting aid, not a measurement — a 12 is not meaningfully worse than a 10.

What goes here: Increasing, Stable or Decreasing since the last review.
Why it earns its place: Often more useful than the rating itself. A moderate risk trending upward usually deserves attention before a high one that is stable.

What goes here: What is being done — or an explicit decision to accept the risk as it stands.
Why it earns its place: Accepting a risk is legitimate. Accepting one without recording that you did is the problem.

What goes here: The named person doing the action. Frequently not the risk owner.
Why it earns its place: Separating the two makes it clear who is accountable for the exposure versus who is doing the work.

What goes here: A real date. If there is no date, it is an intention rather than an action.
Why it earns its place: Actions without dates accumulate silently and make the register look busy while nothing progresses.

What goes here: The date this row was last genuinely looked at.
Why it earns its place: Makes staleness visible at a glance. Sort by this column before a review meeting.

What goes here: Open, In Progress, Accepted, or Closed.
Why it earns its place: Lets you filter the live register without deleting history.

What goes here: Fifteen risks leadership actually knows beats eighty nobody has read. Risks that are not material can live in a functional list rather than the enterprise register.
Quarterly suits most businesses, with an interim review triggered by significant change — a new market, a major system, an acquisition, a serious incident.
A useful meeting covers what has moved, what is overdue and what is new. Reading every row aloud guarantees the meeting becomes an obligation.
Ratings that never change; one name against most of the register; actions with no date; the register being maintained by one person alone.

Column: This template is a starting point, not a standard. Adjust the columns and scales to fit your business — a structure the team will maintain is worth more than a complete one they abandon.
